planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained, limestone-derived or ordinary garden soil in full sun; this cultivar of the Tennessee coneflower (a cedar-glade endemic once federally listed as endangered) tolerates thin, rocky soils that stress most other perennials.

directions: Set divisions or container plants into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where this selection of the rare Tennessee coneflower forms a mounded clump of deep green foliage topped by narrow, purple-rayed, orange-coned flowers from June into September. It is markedly drought tolerant and thrives in the thin, rocky, often limestone-influenced soils of its native cedar-glade habitat, though it adapts to average garden conditions as long as drainage is good. Pollinators visit the long bloom season steadily, and the persistent seed heads feed finches through winter if left standing; established clumps need little more than an occasional spring division to stay vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Hula Dancer is a pale purple coneflower selection with long, softly curved, pendant petals that give the flower an animated, dancing look in a breeze.

directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Hula Dancer bears fragrant, daisy-like flowers with narrow, softly drooping pale pinkish-purple petals swirling around a prominent copper-orange cone, blooming earlier in the season than most Echinacea purpurea cultivars and continuing from summer into fall. It self-sows readily if seed heads are left in place, which also provides valuable winter forage for finches, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought once established. Use it in borders, cottage gardens, or wildflower meadows where its cut flowers and strong pollinator appeal can be enjoyed close up.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Mellow Yellows is a soft light-yellow-flowered purple coneflower selection that does not need extra fertility to perform well.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mellow Yellows resists the usual expectation of coneflower color with soft light-yellow to golden ray petals surrounding a dark orange cone, on a sturdy, vigorous plant well suited to cutting. It mirrors the species' native prairie and open-woodland origins, performing best in lean to average soil without added fertilizer and becoming notably drought tolerant once roots are established. Bees and butterflies work the flowers through the summer season, and the ripening seed heads feed goldfinches and other birds if allowed to stand into fall and winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Happy Star is a sturdy white-flowered purple coneflower selection that pairs well with native grasses.

directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun, where it tolerates part shade as well; Happy Star carries pure white ray petals radiating from a dark central cone on tall, sturdy stems that rarely need staking, extending the coneflower season from midsummer well into fall. It adapts readily to heat, humidity, drought, and lean soil once established, making it a low-fuss choice among taller border perennials. Butterflies and bees nectar at the flowers, hummingbirds visit occasionally, and finches work the seed heads if they are left standing over winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in dry to average, sharply drained soil in full sun; Beebop is a compact selection of dotted horsemint bred for a tighter mounded habit than the wild species.

directions: Plant in dry to average, sharply drained soil in full sun with good air circulation; Beebop forms a dense, aromatic, dark green mound noticeably shorter than typical dotted horsemint, topped by tiered whorls of small pale-yellow, purple-spotted flowers set against showy pink-tinged bracts. Its extended bloom through summer makes it an exceptional magnet for a wide range of native bees and wasps, more so than most other perennials of similar size. The compact habit suits smaller borders and sandy or dry sunny sites where the taller wild species would sprawl, and the cut flowers hold up well in arrangements; it is both drought tolerant and deer resistant once established.
